 Do Mainers really save energy with daylight saving time? | Column 
 To truly save energy, set your thermostat back — not just your clock. 
 Community: 
 Brunswick 
 Posted

 At this time of year, thermostats like these often find themselves at the center of a hot debate in Maine households. (Gregory Rec/Staff Photographer) 
 Now that you’ve set your clock back, look at your thermostat. If its clock is an hour off, every program fires at the wrong time. If it holds the same temperature at 3 a.m. as at noon, it’s doing what many American thermostats do: holding one number whether anyone is home or awake. A basic programmable thermostat that doesn’t adjust for daylight saving time needs you to adjust it. And you need to make sure the temperature isn’t staying the same when those in the household are sleeping, or at noon when people are at work, or at dinner, when everyone is home and in the room.
 This week’s step on the energy pathway is one of the simplest: Set your thermostat back when you’re asleep or away, and raise it during the hours you actually use each space in your home. It costs nothing, needs no contractor, and works whether you rent or own.
 SET BACK AND SAVE
 Daylight saving time comes from the era of incandescent bulbs: Shift the clock so people are awake during more daylight, and they’ll use less energy to see by. Congress adopted it in 1918 to conserve fuel for World War I and extended it into November in 2007.
 The evidence for savings is thin. The U.S. Department of Energy found the 2007 extension saved just 0.03% of the nation’s yearly electricity. In Indiana, which adopted daylight saving time statewide in 2006, economists Matthew Kotchen and Laura Grant studied more than 7 million household electric bills and found residential electricity use rose about 1%, and 2-4% in the fall. Daylight saving time cuts lighting but shifts routines toward colder mornings, when people turn up the heat.
 WHERE YOUR HOME’S ENERGY ACTUALLY GOES
 According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, heating and cooling account for 52% of home energy use, with space heating alone at about 42%. Lighting is now about 6% of household electricity, and shrinking as LEDs take over. Your thermostat controls the biggest slice of energy directly.
 A THERMOSTAT IS ONLY AS SMART AS ITS SCHEDULE
 DOE estimates you can save up to 10% a year on heating and cooling by turning your thermostat back 7-10 F for eight hours a day. The catch: more than two-thirds of EIA survey households with a programmable thermostat never programmed it. Even smart thermostats run on a schedule. If it was set for last winter’s routine, it’s heating your house for times that may not apply this year.
 Advertisement 
 BUILD YOUR WINTER SCHEDULE
 • Sketch your week. Note when your household wakes, leaves, returns, and goes to bed, on weekdays and weekends.
 • Pick your numbers. DOE suggests about 68 F while you’re awake and home, set back by 7-10 F while you sleep or the house is empty. Start smaller and add a degree weekly if needed.
 • Time the warmup. Start the “wake” period 30-60 minutes before you get up.
 • Think room by room. Give each heating zone its own schedule. With ducted systems, leave doors and vents open.
 USE WHATEVER IS ON YOUR WALL
 • Smart thermostat: Review the schedule with fresh eyes, and confirm that the “away” setting actually lowers the temperature.
 • Programmable thermostat: Set the correct time and day. Make sure it isn’t stuck on “hold,” and replace old batteries.
 Advertisement 
 • Manual thermostat: Turn the dial down at bedtime, tied to a nightly habit like locking the door. Note: Many utilities offer rebates on Energy Star-certified smart thermostats.
 • Heat pump: Keep setbacks modest. Recovering from a cold house can trigger costly backup resistance heat. Steam and radiant floor systems also do best with small setbacks.
 A SIDE STEP FOR OUTDOOR LIGHTS
 Any outdoor light on a schedule set months ago is probably running at the wrong hours. Put lights on a photocell or astronomical timer, and trim their hours to when they help someone. Every dark hour saves electricity and helps nocturnal wildlife.
 YOUR 1 STEP THIS WEEK
 Fix your thermostat’s clock, then program a heating-season schedule: about 68 F when people are home and awake, set back by 7-10 F overnight and when the house is empty. In cooling season, flip the logic: about 78 F when home, 7-10 F higher when away. Write the schedule down, and set a reminder to revisit it at the next clock change to adjust the schedule for the new season.
 Sustainable Practice empowers you to protect our planet in practical ways. Share this article with the person in your household who always fixes the microwave clock. Next time, have them adjust the thermostat, too.
